new.name: category_momentum_onset
new.mechanism: Measures whether the user's interest in the candidate's category is rising or fading right now. The single column is a smoothed log ratio of two shares: the category's share of the user's orders in the last 28 days over its share in the 28 days before that, [A-56, A-28). Both blocks have equal length and always lie inside the visible window, so the column no longer depends on window depth the way the old 92-day comparison did. A category the user is buying more often now should pull its products up in the next order. A category whose share collapsed between two adjacent blocks marks an interest that just ended, so its products should drop even when their lifetime counts are high. The value is NULL when either block has no order of the user, or when the user did not buy the category in either block, so a value is only present where a change can actually be observed. The onset column was dropped: it was a duplicate (R2 0.976 to ag_uc_last5_share) and twin-broken.

new.name: user_pace_shift
new.mechanism: Captures the user's current ordering tempo relative to their own norm. The single column is the log ratio of the mean of the last two inter-order gaps to the user's median gap in the window. An accelerating user tends to place small top-ups that repeat the latest items. A slowing user tends to place a full restock with long-cycle items. The trees can use the column as a switch on the pair-level recency features (up_in_last_order, up_last5_share, up_due), which changes the ranking within a query. The column is only defined with at least 3 visible gaps (4 orders), so a NULL has one meaning at every anchor: too few visible orders. It also stops a median of 1 or 2 gaps from passing as a tempo. The overdue column was dropped as a duplicate of ag_uc_due (R2 0.932).

new.name: topup_urgency
new.mechanism: Measures how specifically the user places urgent top-up orders (within 2 days of the previous order) for this product. The first column is the smoothed log lift of the product's top-up share over the user's own top-up rate. This removes the user-level top-up propensity that dominated the old share, which shrank toward a constant. The second column counts the forgotten-item transitions: top-up orders that contain the product when the immediately preceding order did not. A product the user rushes back for right after a basket that lacked it is an essential they run out of or forget. Such products should reappear in the next order, while products that only ride along in big restocks are less sure. Users with no top-up order get no row, so the null stratum is NULL rather than a smoothing constant.

new.name: product_cadence_shift
new.mechanism: For products the user repurchased at least twice in the window (3+ purchases, 2+ gaps), compares the latest repurchase gap with the median of the user's gaps for the product (log ratio). A shrinking latest gap shows the product is being consumed faster now, for example a new household need, so it should rank higher at the next order. A stretched gap shows the habit is fading. With a single gap the ratio is identically 0, so pairs with fewer than 2 gaps now get no row. The since_last_gap column was dropped: it duplicated up_due (R2 0.94) and was twin-broken.

new.name: category_exploration_burst
new.mechanism: Measures whether the user is currently trialing in the candidate's category. The single column is the share of the other products of the category that the user bought in the last 28 days that were new, meaning first seen in the visible window inside those 28 days. The candidate itself is excluded from both counts, which removes the self-inclusion the skeptic found. A user shopping around in a category makes another not-yet-bought product of it more likely and the old favourite less sure. A share of 0 marks a settled, loyal phase. The value is NULL when the user bought no other product of the category in the last 28 days, so it no longer re-encodes category recency (uc_days_since_last). It is also NULL when the user has no visible order before A-28, where every product would read as new.

new.name: item_audience_growth_curve
new.mechanism: Growth or decay of the product audience, measured as the share of weekly active buyers so that swings in total traffic between anchors cancel. One column: the log-linear slope of the weekly buyer share over the last 8 weeks. Changes in response to the critiques: (1) the slope is fitted only on full weeks after the product's first sale in the visible window, so launch timing and zero weeks before launch no longer drive it; (2) it is NULL unless there are at least 4 such weeks and at least 20 weekly buyers in total, so tail noise near the 0.5/n_act floor is excluded; (3) the peak-ratio column is dropped, because it restated staple behaviour (R2 0.771 to ag_p_rebuy14) and a noisy max. Rising products should gain adopters and repeaters in the next 14 days, and decaying ones lose them. The 8-week slope is longer-range and less noisy than the 7/28 ratio in p_trend.

new.name: user_knn_neighbourhood
new.mechanism: User-user neighbourhood collaborative filtering. Each user's seeds are their 15 most-ordered products over the visible 120 days, among products with 2..500 distinct buyers (the distinctive tastes). Neighbours are other users sharing at least 2 seeds. Similarity is an exact integer sum of round(1000/ln(1+buyers)), and the top 50 neighbours are kept. The columns are the similarity-weighted share of neighbours who bought the candidate in the last 28 days, and its log lift over the global 28-day buyer share. Users with the same niche tastes (diet, household type, local assortment) buy similar new items, which lifts non-repeat candidates above plain popularity. Revision: (1) the batch-invariance failure came from ranking the top-50 neighbours on float sums, whose rounding depends on the aggregation plan; similarity is now an integer sum, so the ranking is exact. new.name: personal_cross_transition
new.mechanism: A personal order-to-order transition graph from the user's own 120-day sequence. For each product q in the user's latest order, it counts how often the user's next order, after an order containing q, contained the candidate p (q != p). This count is smoothed toward the user's base rate of p in non-first orders. Only the log lift over that base rate is output. These make p more or less likely given what was just bought, beyond how often p is bought. Revision: the raw transition probability is dropped, because it collapsed to the user's frequency (R2 0.87 to ag_up_decay_share). The twin now keeps the true latest order fixed as the last element and hash-shuffles only the earlier orders. The seeds, qn, the non-last order set and so the coverage are identical to the card; only the successor relation is destroyed.

new.name: retailer_sale_silence
new.mechanism: The base never asks whether a candidate is still on sale where the user shops. A repeat candidate last bought weeks ago may have been delisted or be out of stock at the user's main retailer, and the base cannot tell that from an ordinary lapse. Revised to one column: the expected number of missed sale days. This is the days since the product last sold at the user's main retailer, times the product's sale-day rate there. The rate is distinct sale days of the product divided by distinct days on which the retailer sold anything in the same 90 days. Dividing by the retailer's own active days removes the fixed /90 denominator, which understated rates at early anchors. A product that sells most days and has been silent for a week is effectively gone. A tail product silent for the same time is not unusual. The column is NULL when the product never sold at that retailer. The old default of 90 is dropped, so not-stocked is no longer merged with delisted, and the raw silence-days column, which acted as a popularity proxy, is removed.

new.name: price_tier_fit
new.mechanism: Popularity candidates for users with little product overlap are ranked only by counts, but users keep a stable price tier: budget or premium choices within a category. Each product's index is the log of its 28-day median price relative to its category's median product price. The category is now chosen deterministically as the most frequent category, ties by id equality order. The user's tier is the mean index over the user's distinct products, each product counted once, so repeated staples do not dominate. new.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), ul AS (SELECT user_id, max(last_ts) AS last_ts FROM uo GROUP BY user_id), ds AS (SELECT min(ts) AS start_ts FROM orders), rf AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, min(l.ts) AS first_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN rf.first_ts IS NULL THEN NULL WHEN rf.first_ts < ds.start_ts + INTERVAL 7 DAY THEN -120.0 ELSE epoch(rf.first_ts - ul.last_ts) / 86400.0 END AS f_x_c4_new_since_visit FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ul ON ul.user_id = c.user_id CROSS JOIN ds LEFT JOIN rf ON rf.retailer = um.retailer AND rf.product_id = c.product_id;

twin.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), ul AS (SELECT user_id, max(last_ts) AS last_ts FROM uo GROUP BY user_id), ds AS (SELECT min(ts) AS start_ts FROM orders), rf AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, arg_min(l.ts, hash(l.order_id, l.line_item_id)) AS first_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN rf.first_ts IS NULL THEN NULL WHEN rf.first_ts < ds.start_ts + INTERVAL 7 DAY THEN -120.0 ELSE epoch(rf.first_ts - ul.last_ts) / 86400.0 END AS f_x_c4_new_since_visit_tw FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ul ON ul.user_id = c.user_id CROSS JOIN ds LEFT JOIN rf ON rf.retailer = um.retailer AND rf.product_id = c.product_id;

rival.explanation: New-since-visit may proxy launch promotions (new products are discounted and featured), so the gain would coincide with the promo columns instead of with the user's missed exposure.
rival.stratum: Candidates with a positive 7-day discount share (ag_p_promo7 > 0), for all users

cards.name: category_momentum_onset
cards.mechanism: Measures whether the user's interest in the candidate's category is rising or fading right now. The single column is a smoothed log ratio of two shares: the category's share of the user's orders in the last 28 days over its share in the 28 days before that, [A-56, A-28). Both blocks have equal length and always lie inside the visible window, so the column no longer depends on window depth the way the old 92-day comparison did. A category the user is buying more often now should pull its products up in the next order. A category whose share collapsed between two adjacent blocks marks an interest that just ended, so its products should drop even when their lifetime counts are high. The value is NULL when either block has no order of the user, or when the user did not buy the category in either block, so a value is only present where a change can actually be observed. The onset column was dropped: it was a duplicate (R2 0.976 to ag_uc_last5_share) and twin-broken.
cards.stratum: Candidates with a category, of users with orders in both 28-day blocks, where the category was bought in at least one block: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY)
cards.null_stratum: Users without an order in one of the two blocks, where the column is NULL: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY)
cards.sql: WITH pc AS (SELECT l.product_id, min(l.master_category_id) AS cat FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id), uo AS (SELECT user_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n28, count(*) FILTER (WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS nold FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) AND ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY GROUP BY user_id), uco AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.master_category_id AS cat, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FILTER (WHERE l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS c28, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FILTER (WHERE l.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS cold FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY AND l.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY l.user_id, l.master_category_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN pc.cat IS NOT NULL AND uo.n28 > 0 AND uo.nold > 0 AND COALESCE(uco.c28, 0) + COALESCE(uco.cold, 0) > 0 THEN ln((COALESCE(uco.c28, 0) + 0.5) / (uo.n28 + 1.0)) - ln((COALESCE(uco.cold, 0) + 0.5) / (uo.nold + 1.0)) END AS f_x_c1_uc_momentum_56 FROM cand c LEFT JOIN uo ON uo.user_id = c.user_id LEFT JOIN pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id LEFT JOIN uco ON uco.user_id = c.user_id AND uco.cat = pc.cat

twin.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn_t, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn_h FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), sh AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.order_id, b.ts FROM ord a JOIN ord b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.rn_h = b.rn_t), pc AS (SELECT l.product_id, min(l.master_category_id) AS cat FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id), uo AS (SELECT user_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n28, count(*) FILTER (WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS nold FROM sh WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY GROUP BY user_id), uco AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.master_category_id AS cat, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FILTER (WHERE sh.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS c28, count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FILTER (WHERE sh.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS cold FROM lines l JOIN sh ON sh.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND sh.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 56 DAY GROUP BY l.user_id, l.master_category_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN pc.cat IS NOT NULL AND uo.n28 > 0 AND uo.nold > 0 AND COALESCE(uco.c28, 0) + COALESCE(uco.cold, 0) > 0 THEN ln((COALESCE(uco.c28, 0) + 0.5) / (uo.n28 + 1.0)) - ln((COALESCE(uco.cold, 0) + 0.5) / (uo.nold + 1.0)) END AS f_x_c1_uc_momentum_56_tw FROM cand c LEFT JOIN uo ON uo.user_id = c.user_id LEFT JOIN pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id LEFT JOIN uco ON uco.user_id = c.user_id AND uco.cat = pc.cat

rival.explanation: The gain may come from a recent (56-day) category share that is less diluted than the lifetime uc_share, not from the change between the two blocks.
rival.stratum: Users with long histories, where the recent share differs from the lifetime one: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id) >= 10

cards.name: user_pace_shift
cards.mechanism: Captures the user's current ordering tempo relative to their own norm. The single column is the log ratio of the mean of the last two inter-order gaps to the user's median gap in the window. An accelerating user tends to place small top-ups that repeat the latest items. A slowing user tends to place a full restock with long-cycle items. The trees can use the column as a switch on the pair-level recency features (up_in_last_order, up_last5_share, up_due), which changes the ranking within a query. The column is only defined with at least 3 visible gaps (4 orders), so a NULL has one meaning at every anchor: too few visible orders. It also stops a median of 1 or 2 gaps from passing as a tempo. The overdue column was dropped as a duplicate of ag_uc_due (R2 0.932).
cards.stratum: Users with at least 4 orders in the window: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id) >= 4
cards.null_stratum: Users with at most 3 orders in the window, where the column is NULL: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id) <= 3
cards.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rk FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), g AS (SELECT user_id, rk, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap FROM o WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), s AS (SELECT user_id, count(*) AS ng, median(gap) AS med_gap, avg(gap) FILTER (WHERE rk <= 2) AS recent_gap FROM g GROUP BY user_id) SELECT user_id, ln((recent_gap + 0.25) / (med_gap + 0.25)) AS f_x_c1_u_pace_accel FROM s WHERE ng >= 3

twin.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), g AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap FROM o WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), h AS (SELECT user_id, gap, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS hr FROM g), s AS (SELECT user_id, count(*) AS ng, median(gap) AS med_gap, avg(gap) FILTER (WHERE hr <= 2) AS recent_gap FROM h GROUP BY user_id) SELECT user_id, ln((recent_gap + 0.25) / (med_gap + 0.25)) AS f_x_c1_u_pace_accel_tw FROM s WHERE ng >= 3

rival.explanation: The gain may come from gap irregularity: users with a dispersed gap distribution get extreme values whether or not the recent gaps are the short ones, so the column would proxy for ag_up_gap_cv-like user volatility.
rival.stratum: Users with an irregular history: (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id) >= 6

cards.name: topup_urgency
cards.mechanism: Measures how specifically the user places urgent top-up orders (within 2 days of the previous order) for this product. The first column is the smoothed log lift of the product's top-up share over the user's own top-up rate. This removes the user-level top-up propensity that dominated the old share, which shrank toward a constant. The second column counts the forgotten-item transitions: top-up orders that contain the product when the immediately preceding order did not. A product the user rushes back for right after a basket that lacked it is an essential they run out of or forget. Such products should reappear in the next order, while products that only ride along in big restocks are less sure. Users with no top-up order get no row, so the null stratum is NULL rather than a smoothing constant.
cards.stratum: Repeat candidates of users who placed at least one top-up order in the window: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o1 JOIN orders o2 ON o1.user_id = o2.user_id AND o2.ts > o1.ts AND o2.ts < o1.ts + INTERVAL 2 DAY WHERE o1.user_id = c.user_id) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id)
cards.null_stratum: Users without any top-up order (no row): NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o1 JOIN orders o2 ON o1.user_id = o2.user_id AND o2.ts > o1.ts AND o2.ts < o1.ts + INTERVAL 2 DAY WHERE o1.user_id = c.user_id)
cards.sql: WITH o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, lag(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_oid FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), ot AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, prev_oid, CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NOT NULL AND epoch(ts - prev_ts) < 172800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS topup FROM o), ur AS (SELECT user_id, sum(topup) AS nt, (sum(topup) + 0.5) / (count(*) + 1.0) AS r FROM ot GROUP BY user_id), up AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), j AS (SELECT up.user_id, up.product_id, ot.topup, CASE WHEN ot.topup = 1 AND q.order_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS fg FROM up JOIN ot ON ot.order_id = up.order_id LEFT JOIN up q ON q.user_id = up.user_id AND q.product_id = up.product_id AND q.order_id = ot.prev_oid) SELECT j.user_id, j.product_id, ln(((sum(j.topup) + 2.0 * max(ur.r)) / (count(*) + 2.0)) / max(ur.r)) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_lift, sum(j.fg) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_forgot FROM j JOIN ur ON ur.user_id = j.user_id WHERE ur.nt > 0 GROUP BY j.user_id, j.product_id

twin.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn_t, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn_h FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), sh AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.order_id, b.ts FROM ord a JOIN ord b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.rn_h = b.rn_t), o AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, lag(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_oid FROM sh), ot AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, prev_oid, CASE WHEN prev_ts IS NOT NULL AND epoch(ts - prev_ts) < 172800 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS topup FROM o), ur AS (SELECT user_id, sum(topup) AS nt, (sum(topup) + 0.5) / (count(*) + 1.0) AS r FROM ot GROUP BY user_id), up AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), j AS (SELECT up.user_id, up.product_id, ot.topup, CASE WHEN ot.topup = 1 AND q.order_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS fg FROM up JOIN ot ON ot.order_id = up.order_id LEFT JOIN up q ON q.user_id = up.user_id AND q.product_id = up.product_id AND q.order_id = ot.prev_oid) SELECT j.user_id, j.product_id, ln(((sum(j.topup) + 2.0 * max(ur.r)) / (count(*) + 2.0)) / max(ur.r)) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_lift_tw, sum(j.fg) AS f_x_c1_up_topup_forgot_tw FROM j JOIN ur ON ur.user_id = j.user_id WHERE ur.nt > 0 GROUP BY j.user_id, j.product_id

rival.explanation: Top-up orders are small, so the lift may only mark products typical of small baskets, which ag_p_topup_share and ag_p_basket_rel already capture at the item level.
rival.stratum: Users with a small mean basket: (SELECT avg(n) FROM (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.product_id) AS n FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY l.order_id) z) < 8

cards.name: product_cadence_shift
cards.mechanism: For products the user repurchased at least twice in the window (3+ purchases, 2+ gaps), compares the latest repurchase gap with the median of the user's gaps for the product (log ratio). A shrinking latest gap shows the product is being consumed faster now, for example a new household need, so it should rank higher at the next order. A stretched gap shows the habit is fading. With a single gap the ratio is identically 0, so pairs with fewer than 2 gaps now get no row. The since_last_gap column was dropped: it duplicated up_due (R2 0.94) and was twin-broken.
cards.stratum: Pairs with at least 3 purchases in the window: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 3
cards.null_stratum: Pairs bought at most twice in the window (no row): (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) <= 2
cards.sql: WITH p AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id, l.ts FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), g AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY ts DESC, order_id DESC) AS rk FROM p), q AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, rk, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap FROM g WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), s AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, count(*) AS ng, max(CASE WHEN rk = 1 THEN gap END) AS last_gap, median(gap) AS med_gap FROM q GROUP BY user_id, product_id) SELECT user_id, product_id, ln((last_gap + 0.5) / (med_gap + 0.5)) AS f_x_c1_up_last_gap_rel FROM s WHERE ng >= 2

twin.sql: WITH p AS (SELECT DISTINCT l.user_id, l.product_id, l.order_id, l.ts FROM lines l JOIN cand c ON c.user_id = l.user_id AND c.product_id = l.product_id), g AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, order_id, ts, lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS prev_ts FROM p), q AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, epoch(ts - prev_ts) / 86400.0 AS gap, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, product_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS hr FROM g WHERE prev_ts IS NOT NULL), s AS (SELECT user_id, product_id, count(*) AS ng, max(CASE WHEN hr = 1 THEN gap END) AS last_gap, median(gap) AS med_gap FROM q GROUP BY user_id, product_id) SELECT user_id, product_id, ln((last_gap + 0.5) / (med_gap + 0.5)) AS f_x_c1_up_last_gap_rel_tw FROM s WHERE ng >= 2

rival.explanation: The gain may come from gap dispersion: pairs with one outlier gap get extreme values whichever gap is the latest, so the column would proxy for irregularity (ag_up_gap_cv).
rival.stratum: Pairs with many purchases, where an outlier gap is likely: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.order_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id = c.product_id) >= 4

cards.name: category_exploration_burst
cards.mechanism: Measures whether the user is currently trialing in the candidate's category. The single column is the share of the other products of the category that the user bought in the last 28 days that were new, meaning first seen in the visible window inside those 28 days. The candidate itself is excluded from both counts, which removes the self-inclusion the skeptic found. A user shopping around in a category makes another not-yet-bought product of it more likely and the old favourite less sure. A share of 0 marks a settled, loyal phase. The value is NULL when the user bought no other product of the category in the last 28 days, so it no longer re-encodes category recency (uc_days_since_last). It is also NULL when the user has no visible order before A-28, where every product would read as new.
cards.stratum: Candidates whose category the user bought (another product of it) in the last 28 days, of users with visible orders before A-28: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = c.user_id AND o.ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id <> c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.master_category_id = (SELECT min(l2.master_category_id) FROM lines l2 WHERE l2.product_id = c.product_id))
cards.null_stratum: Candidates whose category the user did not buy in the last 28 days (NULL): NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lines l WHERE l.user_id = c.user_id AND l.product_id <> c.product_id AND l.ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY AND l.master_category_id = (SELECT min(l2.master_category_id) FROM lines l2 WHERE l2.product_id = c.product_id))
cards.sql: WITH pc AS (SELECT l.product_id, min(l.master_category_id) AS cat FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id), uo AS (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) AND ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY GROUP BY user_id), fp AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.master_category_id AS cat, l.product_id, min(l.ts) AS first_ts, max(l.ts) AS last_ts FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY l.user_id, l.master_category_id, l.product_id), x AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE fp.first_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_new, count(*) FILTER (WHERE fp.last_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_act FROM cand c JOIN pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id JOIN uo ON uo.user_id = c.user_id JOIN fp ON fp.user_id = c.user_id AND fp.cat = pc.cat AND fp.product_id <> c.product_id GROUP BY c.user_id, c.product_id) SELECT user_id, product_id, n_new * 1.0 / n_act AS f_x_c1_uc_new_other_share FROM x WHERE n_act > 0

twin.sql: WITH ord AS (SELECT user_id, order_id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, order_id) AS rn_t, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY hash(order_id), order_id) AS rn_h FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), sh AS (SELECT a.user_id, a.order_id, b.ts FROM ord a JOIN ord b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.rn_h = b.rn_t), pc AS (SELECT l.product_id, min(l.master_category_id) AS cat FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY l.product_id), uo AS (SELECT user_id FROM sh WHERE ts < TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY GROUP BY user_id), fp AS (SELECT l.user_id, l.master_category_id AS cat, l.product_id, min(sh.ts) AS first_ts, max(sh.ts) AS last_ts FROM lines l JOIN sh ON sh.order_id = l.order_id WHERE l.master_category_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY l.user_id, l.master_category_id, l.product_id), x AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE fp.first_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_new, count(*) FILTER (WHERE fp.last_ts >= TIMESTAMP '{A}' - INTERVAL 28 DAY) AS n_act FROM cand c JOIN pc ON pc.product_id = c.product_id JOIN uo ON uo.user_id = c.user_id JOIN fp ON fp.user_id = c.user_id AND fp.cat = pc.cat AND fp.product_id <> c.product_id GROUP BY c.user_id, c.product_id) SELECT user_id, product_id, n_new * 1.0 / n_act AS f_x_c1_uc_new_other_share_tw FROM x WHERE n_act > 0

rival.explanation: A high new share may reflect a wide category with many substitutes, or left truncation for users whose base history is much longer than the window, rather than current exploration.
rival.stratum: Large categories with many distinct products: (SELECT count(DISTINCT l.product_id) FROM lines l WHERE l.master_category_id = (SELECT min(l2.master_category_id) FROM lines l2 WHERE l2.product_id = c.product_id)) >= 200

cards.name: item_audience_growth_curve
cards.mechanism: Growth or decay of the product audience, measured as the share of weekly active buyers so that swings in total traffic between anchors cancel. One column: the log-linear slope of the weekly buyer share over the last 8 weeks. Changes in response to the critiques: (1) the slope is fitted only on full weeks after the product's first sale in the visible window, so launch timing and zero weeks before launch no longer drive it; (2) it is NULL unless there are at least 4 such weeks and at least 20 weekly buyers in total, so tail noise near the 0.5/n_act floor is excluded; (3) the peak-ratio column is dropped, because it restated staple behaviour (R2 0.771 to ag_p_rebuy14) and a noisy max. Rising products should gain adopters and repeaters in the next 14 days, and decaying ones lose them. The 8-week slope is longer-range and less noisy than the 7/28 ratio in p_trend.

cards.name: retailer_supply_silence
cards.mechanism: Stock-out or delisting of the product at the user's main retailer. One column: the number of expected sale days that passed without a sale. The rate is shrunk with 7 pseudo-days, so a product sold once is not treated as a daily seller. Using the rate before the silence, not over a window that contains it, separates the measure from plain popularity: a daily seller silent for 4 days scores about 3.5, while a weekly seller silent for 4 days scores about 0.5. Changes in response to the critiques: sale_days14 is dropped (TWIN-BROKEN, retailer popularity). Products never sold at the retailer are now NULL rather than 5.0, so never-stocked is not mixed with silent. The stratum uses the same main retailer as the SQL. The main retailer is computed on the visible 120-day orders with the base tie rules; this is the shelf the user currently shops at, and it may differ from the base main_retailer for users who switched. A next order needs the product on that shelf, so the column should demote repeat candidates the user cannot currently get.

cards.name: hour_band_fit
cards.mechanism: Daily rhythm. Orders are split into six 4-hour bands. The user's band distribution is recency-weighted (weight exp(-age/28 days)) and, as a critic asked, shrunk toward the global band mix with a prior of 3 orders. A single visible order no longer gives a point mass, and users with no visible order fall back to the global mix, which gives exactly 0. The product's lift per band is its share of orders in the band over the global band share, smoothed with a prior of 20 orders to calm tail products. The column is the log of the lift averaged under the user's distribution. Breakfast and fresh items fit morning shoppers, snacks and drinks evening shoppers. The next order will most likely fall in the user's habitual band, so among popular candidates the user never bought, this should promote the ones that match that time of day. The SQL is rewritten in full and visible for audit.

cards.name: item_weekly_overdispersion
cards.mechanism: Robustness of a product's popularity to short-lived bursts. The Pearson chi-square grew with volume (R2 0.632 to p_buyers_28), so it is replaced by the method-of-moments negative-binomial dispersion: alpha = sum((n_w - e_w)^2 - n_w) / sum(e_w^2). Here n_w is the weekly distinct-buyer count and e_w the count expected from each week's active-user traffic. Subtracting n_w removes the Poisson part, and dividing by e_w^2 makes alpha a squared relative fluctuation, invariant to volume in expectation. Weeks are counted only after the product's first sale in the visible window, with the partial launch week excluded, so a launch is not read as a burst. The value is NULL below 4 weeks or 20 buyers, where it would be noise, and clipped at 0. Bursty products (one-off promotions, events) have pop-retailer and global ranks inflated by a temporary wave that will not carry into the next 14 days, so the model can discount source b and c ranks for them.

cards.name: seed_cooc_pmi
cards.mechanism: Measures how specifically the candidate co-occurs in shoppers' baskets with the user's core repertoire, beyond the candidate's popularity. The repertoire is the user's top-10 products in the 120-day window, weighted by distinct orders times exp(-days since the user's last purchase of the seed / 60), so ended interests fade. The co-occurrence graph is built over the last 14 days of all orders. The single column is the log of the seed-weighted lift n_co*N/(n_seed*n_cand), which divides out candidate popularity. Complements of a user's staples (pasta with sauce, cereal with milk) tend to enter the next basket. The existing last_order_copurchase seeds only from the latest order. This card seeds from the stable repertoire, so it also scores complements of habitual items when the last order was a small top-up. Revision: the conditional-probability column is dropped, because it was popularity (R2 0.814 to p_buyers_7, and the twin kept it). The neighbour-shuffled twin cuts the lift to rho 0.198, so the lift is the seed-specific part.

cards.name: user_knn_neighbourhood
cards.mechanism: User-user neighbourhood collaborative filtering. Each user's seeds are their 15 most-ordered products over the visible 120 days, among products with 2..500 distinct buyers (the distinctive tastes). Neighbours are other users sharing at least 2 seeds. Similarity is an exact integer sum of round(1000/ln(1+buyers)), and the top 50 neighbours are kept. The columns are the similarity-weighted share of neighbours who bought the candidate in the last 28 days, and its log lift over the global 28-day buyer share. Users with the same niche tastes (diet, household type, local assortment) buy similar new items, which lifts non-repeat candidates above plain popularity. Revision: (1) the batch-invariance failure came from ranking the top-50 neighbours on float sums, whose rounding depends on the aggregation plan; similarity is now an integer sum, so the ranking is exact. (2) The seeds and the similarity use the full 120-day window instead of 56 days, to reduce the coverage swing between anchors (0.367 vs 0.857).

cards.name: personal_cross_transition
cards.mechanism: A personal order-to-order transition graph from the user's own 120-day sequence. For each product q in the user's latest order, it counts how often the user's next order, after an order containing q, contained the candidate p (q != p). This count is smoothed toward the user's base rate of p in non-first orders. Only the log lift over that base rate is output. It isolates individual rotation habits: alternating two flavours, buying detergent the order after a big fresh order, a rhythm between product groups. These make p more or less likely given what was just bought, beyond how often p is bought. Revision: the raw transition probability is dropped, because it collapsed to the user's frequency (R2 0.87 to ag_up_decay_share). The twin now keeps the true latest order fixed as the last element and hash-shuffles only the earlier orders. The seeds, qn, the non-last order set and so the coverage are identical to the card; only the successor relation is destroyed.

cards.name: retailer_sale_silence
cards.mechanism: The base never asks whether a candidate is still on sale where the user shops. A repeat candidate last bought weeks ago may have been delisted or be out of stock at the user's main retailer, and the base cannot tell that from an ordinary lapse. Revised to one column: the expected number of missed sale days. This is the days since the product last sold at the user's main retailer, times the product's sale-day rate there. The rate is distinct sale days of the product divided by distinct days on which the retailer sold anything in the same 90 days. Dividing by the retailer's own active days removes the fixed /90 denominator, which understated rates at early anchors. A product that sells most days and has been silent for a week is effectively gone. A tail product silent for the same time is not unusual. The column is NULL when the product never sold at that retailer. The old default of 90 is dropped, so not-stocked is no longer merged with delisted, and the raw silence-days column, which acted as a popularity proxy, is removed.

cards.name: price_tier_fit
cards.mechanism: Popularity candidates for users with little product overlap are ranked only by counts, but users keep a stable price tier: budget or premium choices within a category. Each product's index is the log of its 28-day median price relative to its category's median product price. The category is now chosen deterministically as the most frequent category, ties by id equality order. The user's tier is the mean index over the user's distinct products, each product counted once, so repeated staples do not dominate. The candidate itself is left out of the mean, so repeat candidates are not compared with themselves. The column is the absolute gap between the candidate's index and that leave-one-out tier. Because it is a distance, it cannot reduce to the item's own index the way the old signed gap could, and that addresses the item-level rival. The sparse, anchor-unstable within-category column is dropped. Never-bought candidates in the user's tier should rank above off-tier popular items.

cards.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), ul AS (SELECT user_id, max(last_ts) AS last_ts FROM uo GROUP BY user_id), ds AS (SELECT min(ts) AS start_ts FROM orders), rf AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, min(l.ts) AS first_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN rf.first_ts IS NULL THEN NULL WHEN rf.first_ts < ds.start_ts + INTERVAL 7 DAY THEN -120.0 ELSE epoch(rf.first_ts - ul.last_ts) / 86400.0 END AS f_x_c4_new_since_visit FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ul ON ul.user_id = c.user_id CROSS JOIN ds LEFT JOIN rf ON rf.retailer = um.retailer AND rf.product_id = c.product_id;

twin.sql: WITH uo AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.retailer, count(*) AS n_o, max(o.ts) AS last_ts FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY o.user_id, o.retailer), um AS (SELECT user_id, retailer FROM (SELECT user_id, retailer, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY n_o DESC, last_ts DESC, retailer) AS rn FROM uo) x WHERE rn = 1), ul AS (SELECT user_id, max(last_ts) AS last_ts FROM uo GROUP BY user_id), ds AS (SELECT min(ts) AS start_ts FROM orders), rf AS (SELECT o.retailer, l.product_id, arg_min(l.ts, hash(l.order_id, l.line_item_id)) AS first_ts FROM lines l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id WHERE o.retailer IN (SELECT retailer FROM um) AND l.product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM cand) GROUP BY o.retailer, l.product_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.product_id, CASE WHEN rf.first_ts IS NULL THEN NULL WHEN rf.first_ts < ds.start_ts + INTERVAL 7 DAY THEN -120.0 ELSE epoch(rf.first_ts - ul.last_ts) / 86400.0 END AS f_x_c4_new_since_visit_tw FROM cand c JOIN um ON um.user_id = c.user_id JOIN ul ON ul.user_id = c.user_id CROSS JOIN ds LEFT JOIN rf ON rf.retailer = um.retailer AND rf.product_id = c.product_id;

withdrawn.reason: up_rate_trend has R2 0.947 to up_orders_28 and up_old_share has R2 0.843 to up_days_since_first. The base and the agent's decay and streak columns already carry the product-level rise and lapse. The category-level version of the trend idea survives in revised G1-1, with equal-length blocks.

Training anchors are 14 days apart and share one weekday, so the predicted next weekday hardly varies across anchors. The per-weekday counts are about 2, which makes the lift noise. The twin is indistinguishable from the card (R2 0.0431 vs 0.0425, rho 0.174 vs 0.159), so the shuffle does not destroy what the column measures. The fix the critic suggested, predicting from A conditional on no order yet, would still rest on the same noisy counts.

first_sold_days is left-truncated at the window start and is the same column as other cards' product age (identical rho 0.603, R2 0.557 to p_buyers_28). The silence column is a near-monotone popularity transform, and its twin is even closer to popularity, so the shuffle does not destroy it. Both overlap other cards' silence and shelf-age columns. The family lies outside the user-intent lens.

The age column duplicates first_sold_days from another generator: rho 0.603 and R2 0.557 to p_buyers_28, the same values to three decimals. Inside a 120-day window, a late first sale mostly means a rare product, not a launch. The availability share keeps rho 0.453 to p_buyers_28 in its twin, so it is tail popularity. The withheld SQL also cannot be audited. A rate-normalised age would still lean on the same popularity column, so nothing distinct remains.

Abandonment is the complement of an existing repurchase rate: R2 0.932 and 0.79 to ag_p_rebuy14. The hash time-split twin keeps R2 0.965, so the time-local decay is not what the column measures. Cold products get only the prior. No revision separates delisting from the static staple trait.

The signal is very weak (rho <= 0.068) and overlaps C28 next_dow_routine, which covers the upcoming-weekday routine. The weekday of the first order in a 14-day window is poorly predictable without the user's gap, so the column would mostly add noise. The daily-rhythm idea continues in G2-6 with proper shrinkage.

trial_conv28 restates product repurchase (R2 0.892 to p_repeat_share) and is TWIN-BROKEN (0.864). The shift column compares a recent cohort with an old one that, given the 120-day window and the 28-day activity requirement, is limited to [A-92, A-56) and is thin. For most products both cohorts collapse to the prior, so the shift is noise. Cold launches, the intended target, are excluded by construction.

The twin is broken: the hash-ordered lag keeps rho 0.910 on prob, so the sequence carries nothing. prob is popularity (R2 0.887 to p_buyers_7). The twin lift has nearly the same profile as the card lift (R2 0.43 vs 0.445 to ag_co_last_lift). At 25 s of a 40 s budget it costs too much for a column that duplicates existing features.

The twin is broken. The time-shuffled twin keeps |rho_wq| at 0.999 (prob) and 0.955 (lift), so the order-to-order transition carries no information: the value is static household category affinity, as the rival says. prob also duplicates ag_uc_rebuy_bucket (R2 0.886).

It ran out of memory on both probe anchors (card on day 2, twin on day 1), and took 27.8 s even where it ran. Where it ran, both columns were largely explained by existing features: lift R2 0.752 to ag_uc_last_pick, transition R2 0.729 to ag_uc_orders_after. Coverage is limited to categories the user already bought, where the base is already strong, so a capped rewrite is unlikely to add a non-redundant signal.

The current-state column duplicates ag_up_streak (R2 0.905). The gap column is largely explained by ag_up_orders_since (R2 0.72). Coverage is only 0.354, swings 0.216 to 0.491 between anchors, and covers only candidates already bought in the window, where the base is strongest. The alternation hypothesis is better tested through the kept personal-transition lift (G3-6) than through a near-duplicate column.

Batch invariance is red. Beyond that, the time-shuffled twin reproduces the card's profile (share rho 0.45 vs 0.458 to popr_rank, lift 0.252 vs 0.273, same coverage), so the 'what comes after a similar basket' path adds nothing over local-assortment similarity. The neighbourhood idea is kept in the revised user kNN (G3-3), which has the stronger, non-sequential mechanism; keeping both would add a redundant column.

The adopt column is popularity: R2 0.97 to p_buyers_28, and it keeps |rho_wq| 0.998 with its twin (TWIN-BROKEN). The keep column has R2 0.88 to ag_p_next_reorder. The 'newcomer' cohort is also contaminated by dormant returners whose earlier orders fall before the visible 120-day window, and an item-level column cannot target newcomers by itself. Nothing specific to newcomers is left.

TWIN-BROKEN: longgap_return keeps |rho_wq| 0.851 with the time-shuffled twin, so it measures tenure and order density inside the 120-day window, not rotation behaviour. rebuy_gap_med has R2 0.822 to up_mean_interval, and its non-NULL share swings from 0.37 to 0.827 across anchors. Both columns repeat existing cadence features and are right-censored by the window.
